loadNamespace("duckdb")

THIP's inpatient tables are records of real people's stays in hospital.
Handling them well protects those people, keeps your access to THIP, and makes
your results worth trusting. This guide covers what THIP's conditions ask of
you and the working habits that follow from them: what to take out of THIP,
small counts, credentials, and the decisions that belong to your protocol.

## What THIP's conditions say

The conditions, in short:

- THIP is an information system for study and research: it opens health data,
  as a data warehouse, to agencies involved in research in Thailand.
- Ownership of the data stays with the agency that owns them. Data brought in
  by research projects belong to the agency that funded or carried out the
  research, and research data belong to the researcher's institution and the
  researcher.
- Use the system honestly and ethically, and only within your role.
- Log in for the first time within two weeks of approval.
- Do not share your account or your password with anyone.
- When you want to download data, attach your institution's research-ethics
  approval in full.
- THIP may check the details you register with, and may cancel your membership
  if they are wrong, or your access if you use it outside its purpose or its
  conditions.

You accept them when you register for a THIP account (the terms shown at
sign-up); read them there, in THIP's own words. The rest of this guide is about
keeping to them while you work.

## Keep records inside THIP

Your analysis runs inside THIP's notebook platform, where the records are. Take
out only what your approved protocol allows. Usually that means aggregate
tables, such as counts, percentages and model estimates, rather than records or
identifiers such as `pid` and `tran_id`. Taking out means more than
downloading: a table copied into a document, a screenshot and a notebook that
kept its output all leave THIP too.

thipR is built for this way of working. Queries run on the database, and only
what you print or `collect()` comes into your R session, which on THIP runs
inside your account. The checks in [Check before you trust](data-checks.html)
bring back counts, and data frames of records, such as `candidates` in [From
question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html), stay in that session.

Two habits help:

- **Look before anything leaves.** Read each table as a stranger would: does it
  hold an identifier, the dates of one person's stay, or a count so small that
  it points to someone?
- **Clear a notebook's output before you share it.** A notebook keeps what it
  printed, so one that printed records carries them wherever it goes.

## Small counts

A small count can point to a few people, especially beside a place, an age group
or a month. A protocol usually sets the smallest count you may show, and how to
show smaller ones, for example as `<10`. Take the threshold from your protocol,
and follow THIP's rule as well where it sets one; this course does not choose a
number.

As an example, count the records of fiscal year 2567 by discharge status
(`dischs`) in the example database:

```{r by-status}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- thip_connect_example()

by_status <- tbl(con, "nhso2567") |>
  count(dischs, name = "records") |>
  arrange(dischs) |>
  collect()
```

Set the threshold once, as a variable, and replace every count below it before
the table leaves THIP. The other counts become text too, so write them with
`format()`, which keeps them in full (`as.character()` would turn 100000 into
`1e+05`):

```{r suppress}
min_count <- 10  # set this from your protocol

by_status |>
  mutate(records = if_else(
    records < min_count,
    paste0("<", min_count),
    format(records, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  ))
```

The count for discharge status
`r by_status$dischs[by_status$records < min_count]`, not delivered, was below
`r min_count` and now reads `r paste0("<", min_count)`.

Hiding one cell is not always enough. If your report also gives the year's
total, `r format(sum(by_status$records), big.mark = ",")` records, anyone can
subtract the `r sum(by_status$records >= min_count)` counts shown and find the
hidden one. Hide a second cell too, or leave the total out, as your protocol
says; the same goes for a percentage of a known total. The summary in the
[Worked example](getting-started.html) is a case in point: both of its
readmitted counts are below 10. Apply the rule last, to the tables you will
show: inside THIP, keep the full counts for your analysis.

## Credentials stay out of code

Your THIP account and password are yours alone, as THIP's conditions say. The
database username and password that thipR uses are credentials too, and they
belong in one place: the settings file that `thip_setup()` writes. Run
`thip_setup()` once in your THIP account, as [Start
here](start-here.html#configure-once-connect-each-session) shows. It asks for
the password in a masked box and saves the connection settings in a file only
your account (and the server's administrators) can read; from then on,
`thip_connect()` reads them from there.

- Never type a password into a notebook cell or a script, even for a moment:
  notebooks keep their cells and output, and code gets copied.
- Keep the settings file, `.Renviron` in your home folder, out of repositories
  and shared folders. It is plain text, protected only by its file permissions.
- Do not print the settings or lend them: a colleague who needs THIP needs
  their own account.

## thipR only reads

thipR connects read-only. Every query it sends asks the database for read-only
access, and it never creates, changes or deletes a table. When it needs your
people on the database, as `thip_window()` does, it sends them inside the query
instead of writing a table ([Look back and follow
up](look-back-follow-up.html#the-round-trip)). Keep your own code the same way:
when dplyr suggests its `copy` argument to join a data frame to a database
table, use `thip_window()` instead ([Working with a database from
R](database-from-r.html#join-tables-on-the-same-connection)).

## Decisions that are yours

thipR gives you tools, not study decisions. It does not choose:

- **Clinical definitions:** which codes mean appendicitis or diabetes. The code
  lists in this course illustrate the methods; they are not validated
  definitions.
- **Eligibility:** who can enter the study, from which dates and at which ages.
- **Repeated records and damaged values:** what to do with records that appear
  twice, dates that cannot be read and impossible values ([Check before you
  trust](data-checks.html)).

These are your protocol's decisions. Make them before you look at results,
write them down with the code lists you used and where they came from, and
report them with your findings.

The example's numbers, such as the readmission percentages in the [Worked
example](getting-started.html), are invented ([Meet the THIP
data](meet-the-data.html)): never present them as findings, and say so when you
teach with them.

## Report problems

For a problem with thipR or with these guides, open an issue on
[GitHub](https://github.com/Songyosr/thipR/issues). Issues are public, so leave
out passwords and other credentials, THIP's host names and addresses, and
results from real THIP data, counts included. Show the problem on the example
database instead: `thip_connect_example()` runs the same code, so you can share
the code and its output. For a problem with your THIP account or with THIP's
data, contact the THIP team.

## In short

- You accept THIP's conditions at sign-up: the data stay their owners', your
  account is yours alone, downloads need your institution's ethics approval,
  and THIP may cancel access used outside its conditions.
- Work inside THIP, and take out only what your protocol allows: usually
  aggregate tables.
- Hide counts below your protocol's threshold, and anything that would let
  someone work them out.
- Keep credentials in the file `thip_setup()` writes, never in code or
  notebooks.
- thipR only reads. Clinical definitions, eligibility and repeated records are
  your protocol's decisions.
- The example's numbers are invented: never present them as findings.
- Report thipR problems on GitHub, without credentials, addresses or results
  from real data.

This is the last guide in the course.
